 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

        Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC” and together with Oncor, the “Applicants”) respectfully file this brief

on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (“Brief”) related to the transmission projects hereinafter

called the “Import Path 2 Projects,” comprised of the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill

Substation 765 kV transmission line project and the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765

kV transmission line project. The Import Path 2 Projects were identified by the Electric Reliability

Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) approved by

the Commission in two orders dated October 5, 2024 and April 24, 2025 in Project No. 55718.

        This Brief is filed pursuant to SOAH Order No. 35, which requires Applicants to submit a

brief on remanded Issue Nos. 11 and 13 by October 7, 2026. 1 This Brief supplements Applicants’

Directory of Record Evidence of Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (“Directory of

Evidence”), which Applicants filed on September 21, 2026. 2 The Directory of Evidence collects,

by issue, the primary record exhibits and hearing transcript excerpts related to Issue Nos. 11 and

13. A copy of the Directory of Evidence is attached to this Brief as Exhibit A and is incorporated

herein by reference for all purposes.

        The purpose of this Brief is to clarify two points supported by the record evidence: (1) the

proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards (Issue

11); and (2) while a congestion cost savings analysis is not required for reliability projects, the

record evidence shows the Import Path 2 Projects will benefit consumers (Issue 13).

     I.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11

           Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
           reliability standards?

           Yes. The record evidence is clear that the Import Path 2 Projects are necessary to meet

state and federal reliability standards established by the North American Electric Reliability

Corporation (“NERC”) and state standards established by ERCOT planning criteria.                                  An

affirmative answer to Issue No. 11 necessarily informs the need analysis under PURA

§ 37.056(c)(1)–(2) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii); a project required to cure NERC reliability

violations is, by definition, needed to provide reliable service.

           Federal law requires that the bulk power system be planned to operate reliably. 3 NERC is

authorized by federal law to develop and enforce mandatory reliability standards. 4 ERCOT is

subject to these standards as the region’s planning authority registered with NERC. Thus, ERCOT

must conduct planning studies under these mandatory NERC reliability standards. ERCOT’s study

of the Permian Basin under those standards revealed that the existing system does not meet them—

identifying thermal overloads, voltage instability, and future conditions the system simply cannot

support. 5 This is a reliability standard violation that requires a solution. The PBRP, and the Import

Path 2 Projects within it, were the solution recommended to correct those NERC reliability

violations. 6 The sections that follow walk through the supporting record evidence in more detail.

             In the wake of the 2003 Northeast blackout, Congress replaced a system of largely

voluntary reliability guidelines with mandatory and enforceable reliability standards, authorizing

NERC to develop and enforce those standards for the bulk power system in the United States.

NERC is the federally authorized organization responsible for developing and enforcing

mandatory reliability standards for the bulk power system in the United States. 7 NERC Reliability

Standard TPL-001-5.1, titled “Transmission System Planning Performance Requirements,” is one

of the specific standards relevant here, and the reliability assessments that ERCOT performed were

based on this reliability standard as well as the ERCOT Nodal Protocols and ERCOT Planning

Criteria. 8 Under this standard, ERCOT transmission planners study future system needs by

simulating different contingency scenarios, including equipment failures and generation outages. 9

If those studies show that the system cannot continue to operate reliably due to thermal overloads,

voltage instability, and/or an unsolvable power-flow condition, a violation is present and the

standard requires corrective action. 10

            In practical terms, a thermal overload means transmission circuits are carrying more power

than they are physically rated to handle, risking excessive sag, overheating, damage, and failure. 11

Voltage instability means the system cannot maintain acceptable voltage levels, which can lead to

interruptions to end use customer operations and forced outages on the transmission and

downstream distribution systems. 12 An unsolvable power-flow contingency means that, under a

           B. The PBRP Identified Reliability Criteria Violations

           The Import Path 2 Projects originate from the PBRP, which ERCOT developed pursuant

to House Bill 5066 (“H.B. 5066”). 19 As described in Section A above, in developing the PBRP,

ERCOT performed reliability studies in accordance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-

5.1, the ERCOT Planning Guide, and the ERCOT Nodal Protocols. 20 Those studies revealed

serious reliability problems:

           •      ERCOT’s steady-state analysis observed thermal overloads, voltage instability, and

                  unsolvable power-flow contingencies in the 2030 and 2038 study cases. 21

           •      ERCOT observed voltage instability in the 2038 case under N-0 (system intact)

                  conditions in the Delaware Basin area, which includes counties that would be crossed

                  and served by the Import Path 2 Projects. 22

           •      These findings constitute reliability criteria violations under NERC Reliability

                  Standard TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria. The Import Path 2 Projects, in

                  conjunction with other PBRP projects, will resolve these violations. 23

            The reliability need for these Import Path 2 Projects is further confirmed by studies that

have occurred since the PBRP was published. In September 2025, ERCOT established two GTCs

on existing 345 kV transmission lines serving the Far West Texas region (the “Far West Texas

Import GTCs”). 24 As noted above, these GTCs are designated IROLs under NERC Reliability

Standard FAC-011-4; if exceeded or violated, they could result in cascading outages and load shed

exceeding 2,000 MW. 25

           ERCOT’s April 2026 GTC exit strategy identifies all three 765 kV import paths (including

Import Path 2) as essential to retiring those GTCs by 2030, even assuming that approximately

2,500 MW of planned dispatchable generation in the Permian Basin materializes. 26 This is not a

theoretical concern—this is a tangible threat to reliability in the region. Mr. Martin testified that

the Far West Texas Import GTCs are routinely approaching their operating limits even at current

load levels, and that because generation redispatch and transmission reconfiguration cannot solve

the problem, firm load shed is the only remaining option if those limits are exceeded. 27 Thus,

failure to build Import Path 2 eliminates the solution to ERCOT’s identified FAC-011-4 violation.

These constraints are limiting the reliable operation of the grid today and will only worsen as load

continues to grow without the infrastructure recommended in the PBRP.

       F. The ALJs Should Propose Findings of Fact Consistent with the Commission’s
          Recent Orders

       The record establishes a reliability need for the Import Path 2 Projects based on the PBRP

and subsequent ERCOT studies. Accordingly, the supplemental PFD should include the following

finding of fact on Issue 11:

   •   The proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state and federal reliability

       standards, including NERC Reliability Standards TPL-001-5.1 and FAC-011-4 and

       ERCOT planning criteria.


       The Commission has also now approved Import Paths 1 and 3 on findings drawn from the

same PBRP in this record. Therefore, Applicants respectfully propose that the supplemental PFD

include the following findings of fact already adopted in the Commission’s prior orders for Import

Paths 1 and 3.

   •   In the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, ERCOT reported that the Permian Basin had already

       experienced unprecedented load growth and that, based on data provided by the TSPs, the

       electric demand driven by oil and gas development in the Permian Basin was expected to

       continue growing over the next 15 years.

   •   A 2022 load forecast developed by S&P Global projected growth in peak oil-and-gas

       related demand of 11,964 MW in 2030 and 14,705 MW in 2038.

   •   The TSPs also provided demand projections indicating an exponential increase in non-oil

       and gas loads in the Permian Basin region, primarily consisting of demand related to

       cryptocurrency mining operations, data centers, and hydrogen electrolysis facilities. The

        In short, Issue 11 must be answered in the affirmative based on the weight of the record

evidence. ERCOT studied the Permian Basin under mandatory NERC standards, found that the

existing system to violate those standards, and identified the Import Path 2 Projects to resolve

those failures. The Far West Texas Import GTCs show that the problem exists on the grid today,

not just in a forecast. ERCOT reached the same conclusion in the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, the 2025

RTP, and its April 2026 GTC exit strategy, and the Commission has approved Import Paths 1 and

3 on the same reliability foundation. Because the Import Path 2 Projects are required to resolve

violations of NERC reliability standards and ERCOT planning criteria, they are, by definition,
